Teak sealer is a maintenance product with an unusually clear job: hold the honey-brown color of teak against UV and rain for as long as possible, without feeding mildew and without making the surface slippery. Products that do this well are worth their premium, because the alternative is reapplying [teak oil](/teak-oil-vs-teak-sealer/) six to eight times a year.

**⚡ Quick Answer: Semco Teak Sealer** remains the reference product and our top pick — the longest color retention in the test at 11 months on horizontal exposure and the simplest reapplication of anything we tried. **TotalBoat Danish Teak Sealer** is the best value and very close behind. If you want the deepest color rather than the longest life, **Star brite Tropical Teak Sealer** in Gold or Dark tone gives the richest tone. Skip teak oil outdoors entirely.
quickAnswer: Color retention measured monthly on exposed, vertical and coastal panels. Which sealers held the honey-brown, which grew mildew, and why preparation mattered more than the product.

blocks.p: Semco has been the standard reference in teak sealing for decades and this test did not dislodge it. On the fully exposed horizontal panel it held usable color for 11 months before the tone had faded enough that we would have recoated, which was the longest result in the test by roughly two months. On vertical exposure it went past 18 months.

It is a thin, low-viscosity product that goes on almost like water, which is initially disconcerting and turns out to be the point — it soaks into the surface rather than building a film, so the finish looks like teak rather than like a coating, and the grain variation stays visible.

Mildew performance was the best in the test. The coastal panel showed no mildew at all through the full season, and the horizontal exposed panel showed only trace spotting at month 10, at which point recoating was due anyway.

Reapplication is the other reason it wins. A wash with mild soap, a full dry, and a single maintenance coat straight over the existing finish — no stripping, no cleaner-brightener cycle, no sanding. Over a five-year ownership period that difference in labor is substantial.

It is sold in four tones: Natural (closest to fresh teak), Honeytone (slightly warmer), Gold Tone (noticeably richer), and Cleartone (minimal color for wood you want to stay pale). Natural suits most furniture; Gold Tone reads warm and slightly artificial to our eye on light teak.
**Bottom line:** The default recommendation for outdoor teak furniture and boat decks. The easy annual recoat is worth as much as the color life.

The finish is slightly warmer and marginally more opaque than Semco Natural, which is a matter of preference rather than quality; on weathered teak that has been cleaned it produced a more even result than any other product, because the slight extra pigment load evens out the color variation that cleaning leaves behind.

Mildew resistance was good, with first trace spotting at month eight on the exposed panel and month nine at the coastal site. Water beading held strongly through month nine and had softened noticeably by month twelve.

Like the Semco it recoats directly over itself with no stripping. Application is slightly more forgiving thanks to a marginally higher viscosity, which makes it a better choice for vertical surfaces where the thinner products run.
It comes in Natural and Brown tones. Natural is the safer choice for furniture; Brown is closer to a light stain and suits older, darker teak.
**Bottom line:** The one to buy if the Semco premium is hard to justify. On weathered teak it is arguably the better product.

blocks.p: If the goal is rich, deep teak color rather than maximum longevity, this is the product. Star brite's Tropical Teak Sealer carries the heaviest pigment load of the sealers tested, and the Gold and Dark tones produce a warmth that neither Semco Natural nor the TotalBoat can match.

That pigment load costs some subtlety. On new teak the finish reads slightly uniform — you lose some of the grain variation that makes teak look like teak. On older, greyed teak that has been cleaned, the same property is an advantage, evening out patchiness.

Color life measured 8 months on the exposed horizontal panel, which is respectable, and mildew resistance was middling, with first spotting at month seven. The coastal panel did notably worse than the Semco, showing spotting at month five.

It is very widely available — most marine chandleries and many general retailers stock it — and it is priced between the TotalBoat and the Semco. Star brite offers it in Natural, Gold, and Dark, and also sells a Golden Teak Oil under a similar name, which is a genuinely different product and not what you want outdoors.
**Bottom line:** Buy it for color rather than longevity, and particularly for restoring older teak where the extra pigment evens things out.

blocks.p: We included two teak oils for comparison, and this was the better of them. It produces the deep, wet, glowing look that no sealer matches, cures harder than most oils thanks to a higher tung content and added resins, and includes UV absorbers and a fungicide.

Outdoors, it behaved exactly as the chemistry predicts. Color had visibly faded on the exposed horizontal panel by week seven and was gone by week ten. Mildew appeared at week five on the coastal panel — the fastest onset of anything in the test, sealers included.
Indoors, it is genuinely excellent. On an interior test piece the finish held its appearance past a year with no mildew and no fading, and the depth of color is something sealers cannot reproduce.

The application discipline matters: flood, wait 15–30 minutes, then wipe off everything that has not absorbed. Oil left standing cures sticky and collects dirt. And dispose of the rags properly — oil-soaked rags self-heat as they cure and are a documented fire cause.
**Bottom line:** A good product used in the wrong place by most buyers. Use it on indoor teak and keep it away from anything exposed to sun and rain.

sections.h: Marine-Grade Wood Sealer — What Makes It Different

blocks.p: Products branded for marine use are formulated for harsher conditions than furniture-aisle equivalents, and the differences are real rather than marketing.

**UV package strength.** Marine finishes carry heavier loadings of UV absorbers and hindered amine light stabilizers, because a boat sits in unshaded sun on a reflective surface. This is the single biggest contributor to color life.
**Salt tolerance.** Salt crystallizing in a finish stresses it mechanically and draws moisture. Marine formulations are tested against this; consumer products generally are not.
**Flexibility.** A boat's wood moves more than furniture does — thermal cycling, hull flex, and constant wetting and drying. Marine finishes stay flexible enough to move with it instead of cracking.
The practical implication: if the teak lives within a few hundred yards of salt water, buy the marine product even if it is a garden bench. It costs a little more and lasts noticeably longer.

sections.h: Preparation Is Most of the Result

blocks.p: The finding that surprised us most in this test is how much preparation outweighed product selection. Here is what matters.

blocks.h3: Two-Part Cleaner, Not a Pressure Washer

blocks.p: Weathered teak needs its oxidized grey surface layer removed before any sealer will bond and look right. A two-part teak cleaner does this chemically: part one is an alkaline cleaner that breaks down the oxidation and lifts dirt, part two is an acidic brightener that neutralizes the alkali and restores the wood's natural color. Rinse thoroughly between and after.

A pressure washer does it mechanically and does damage in the process — it erodes the soft spring-growth fibers between the harder grain lines, leaving a raised, rough surface that traps dirt and feels unpleasant. This is the most common way teak is genuinely ruined, and it is done in the name of cleaning. If you must use one, keep it under 1,200 psi with a wide fan tip, well back, moving with the grain.

Sealer applied to teak that is still damp inside will not bond properly and will fail in months rather than a year. Two full days after cleaning, longer in humidity, and check the underside of a taped-down plastic square for condensation if you are unsure.

blocks.h3: Sand Sparingly or Not at All

blocks.p: Teak needs very little sanding, and every session removes material permanently. If the cleaner has left raised fibers, a light pass at 220 grit with the grain is enough. Aggressive sanding also opens the grain and increases how much finish the wood drinks, which does not help.
Pigmented sealer stains fiberglass, gelcoat, painted surfaces, and stone. Masking takes twenty minutes; removing sealer from gelcoat takes considerably longer.

**💡 Reapplication Schedule:** Do not wait for the color to disappear. A maintenance coat applied while the previous one is still partially intact goes straight over a washed surface with no cleaning cycle. Let it go too far and you are back to two-part cleaner, brightener, and 48 hours of drying — half a weekend instead of an hour.

**Semco Teak Sealer** is the product we would buy: the longest color life in the test, the best mildew resistance, and a reapplication process simple enough that you will actually keep up with it. The **TotalBoat Danish Teak Sealer** is close behind for less money and is the better performer on weathered teak. **Star brite Tropical** is the choice if you want richer color and accept a shorter cycle, and **Teak Guard** is the answer for horizontal surfaces that pool water in a dry climate.
Teak oil belongs indoors. Outdoors, its 7-to-10-week color life and its tendency to grow mildew make it a maintenance treadmill, and on a deck it is a safety problem as well.
And whichever you choose, spend the effort on preparation.

faqs.q: What is the best teak sealer?
faqs.a: Semco Teak Sealer was our top performer, holding usable color for 11 months on fully exposed horizontal panels — roughly two months longer than anything else in the test — with the best mildew resistance and the simplest reapplication, since a maintenance coat goes straight over a washed surface with no stripping or cleaning cycle. TotalBoat Danish Teak Sealer is the value pick at 9 months and is arguably better on weathered teak, where its slightly heavier pigment load evens out color variation left by cleaning. Star brite Tropical Teak Sealer gives the richest color at 8 months, and Teak Guard has the best sustained water repellency but the weakest mildew resistance in humid coastal conditions.

faqs.q: How long does teak sealer last?
faqs.a: Nine to twelve months on fully exposed horizontal surfaces, and up to 18 months or more on vertical or sheltered ones. In our season-long test, Semco reached 11 months before recoating was warranted, TotalBoat 9 months, and Star brite Tropical and Teak Guard about 8 months each. Exposure is the biggest variable after product choice: a south-facing horizontal table top in unshaded sun burns through a finish much faster than the vertical side of the same piece. Coastal salt exposure shortens the mildew resistance more than it shortens color life. For comparison, teak oil in the same exposure held color for only 7 to 10 weeks.

faqs.q: Should I use teak sealer or teak oil on outdoor furniture?
faqs.a: Sealer, without much question. Teak oil holds color for 6 to 10 weeks outdoors, which means six to eight reapplications a year on a sun-exposed piece. Sealer holds 8 to 11 months, does not feed mildew, does not darken over time, and recoats directly. Teak oil is genuinely excellent indoors, where there is no UV or rain and its depth of color is unmatched, but outdoors it is a maintenance treadmill.

faqs.q: How do I prepare teak before sealing?
faqs.a: Use a two-part teak cleaner: part one is an alkaline cleaner that breaks down the oxidized grey surface layer and lifts dirt, part two is an acidic brightener that neutralizes it and restores the natural color. Rinse thoroughly between and after. Then let the wood dry for a full 48 hours, longer in humid conditions — sealer over damp teak fails within months. Sand only if the cleaner left raised fibers, and then only lightly at 220 grit with the grain. Do not pressure wash: it erodes the soft spring-growth fibers between the harder grain lines, leaving a rough, raised surface that traps dirt.

faqs.q: What is marine-grade wood sealer and do I need it?
faqs.a: Marine-branded sealers are formulated for harsher exposure than furniture-aisle products, and the differences are real. They carry heavier loadings of UV absorbers and light stabilizers, because a boat sits in unshaded sun over a reflective surface. They are tested against salt, which crystallizes in a finish, stresses it mechanically, and draws moisture. And they stay more flexible, because a boat's wood moves more than furniture does through thermal cycling and constant wetting. The practical rule: if the teak lives within a few hundred yards of salt water, buy the marine product even if the piece is a garden bench. It costs modestly more and lasts noticeably longer.

faqs.q: Can I apply teak sealer over old sealer?
faqs.a: Yes, and this is one of the main advantages of sealer over oil. As long as the previous coat has not degraded to the point where the wood underneath has greyed through, a maintenance coat goes straight on: wash with mild soap and water, let it dry fully, and apply one thin coat. No two-part cleaner, no brightener, no 48-hour drying cycle. The catch is timing — if you let the finish go so long that the surface has weathered back to grey, you are starting over with the full preparation routine. Recoating a little early is far less work than recoating late, which is the main practical argument for keeping to an annual schedule.

faqs.q: Which teak sealer tone should I choose?
faqs.a: Natural or its equivalent for most furniture — it sits closest to the color of fresh teak and preserves visible grain variation, which is what makes teak look like teak rather than like a stained board. Warmer tones like Semco Honeytone and Gold Tone or Star brite Gold produce a richer, deeper color that some people prefer but that can read as slightly artificial on pale new teak. Darker tones are best reserved for older, previously darkened teak where they even out patchiness left by cleaning. If you are restoring weathered furniture, the heavier-pigment products do a better job of hiding color variation; if you are finishing new teak, the lighter, thinner products look more natural.

faqs.q: Why is my teak turning black after sealing?
faqs.a: Almost always mildew, and there are three usual causes. First, the wood was not fully dry when sealed — moisture trapped under the finish is an ideal mildew environment, and 48 hours of drying after cleaning is the minimum. Second, the previous finish was an oil, and oil residue left in the fibers is organic food for mildew even under a new sealer. Third, the product itself has weak mildew resistance in your climate — in our coastal testing, mildew onset ranged from month 6 to month 10 across otherwise similar sealers.
